title: Stand the night
hookLine: O you wrapped in garments, stand in the night, except a little (73:1–2)

cards: It's the middle of the night. The house is asleep. You're under a heavy blanket, pulled up to your chin, the warmest you've been all day.
And someone speaks to you, gently, by the name of what you're doing. You, wrapped up. Get up.
Not all night. Most of it, or half, or a little less. That is how surah seventy-three begins.
It's addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it calls him by his blanket: al-muzzammil, the one wrapped up.

teach.b: Verses one and two, in Pickthall's translation: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment! Keep vigil the night long, save a little." Verses three and four make it flexible: half the night, or a little less, or a little more.

Some commentators hear the name as tender: not a formal title but a description, almost a nickname. They note that Arabs sometimes addressed someone by what they were doing at that moment, as a kind of affection.
Some connect the wrapping to the beginning of revelation.
Sahih al-Bukhari tells how, after the first revelation in the cave of Hira, the Prophet came home shaking and said to his wife Khadijah: wrap me, wrap me.
Commentators differ on whether this surah came right after that, but it is counted among the early ones. Then the call: stand. Qiyam al-layl, standing the night in prayer.
Verse six says why: rising by night is stronger for the heart and more fitting for words.
The night is quieter. Nobody's watching. Your phone, ideally, is face down.
Words said at two in the morning tend to be meant. Verse five gives another reason: We are about to send down on you a weighty word.

Before the heavy work of carrying the message in daylight, the Prophet was given the training of the night. Today this is often called tahajjud, voluntary prayer after sleep, in the last part of the night.
Some do it every night, some during Ramadan, some only now and then. The invitation is the same: get up from the blanket, and stand.

how: Some Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer in units of two rak'ahs, after sleeping and before dawn; some keep it nightly, others mostly in Ramadan or now and then, following the call of al-Muzzammil and the Prophet's practice.

o: the angel who brought the first revelation
the one who memorized the whole Qur'an by heart
the one wrapped up, called to rise and pray at night

games.q: you're wrapped in a warm blanket in the middle of the night. the call comes: stand. how much of the night does 73:2–4 ask for?
o: half, a bit less, or a bit more.
games.why: all night except a little: half, a little less, or a little more. the call is flexible, and gentle.

practice: Sit as if it were the middle of the night: lower the lights if you can, let the house go quiet in your mind, and notice how your attention changes when nobody needs anything from you.
If you pray, you might rise tonight or before dawn for two short units, two rak'ahs, even if it's only once this week.

wordCard.voice: Al-muzzammil. The one wrapped up: in 73:1–2 the Prophet, under his blanket, is called to rise and pray through the night, all but a little. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 73:1: O you wrapped up. al-muzzammil, the one wrapped in garments.

carryVoice: Your line: stand in the night. The night comes first, then the heavy work of the day. See you tomorrow.
